title: How Much, How Many, Which Way
overview: Buy what you need, and find your way to it. Say how much and how many: a few packets, a little flour. Use each and every for one at a time and for all of them. Then say which way a thing goes: into the shop, across the road, past the bank.
learningPath: The lesson: listen once, then listen again with the page open.
Words: 30 words in four groups. Listen, say, check.
Patterns: 3 cards. Read the worked example before the practice.
Reading: a short account, an information text and a shop notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen back. Use the checklist.
Writing: 4 tasks. Compare each one with the model.
Practice: 6 sets. Mark them with the key and count.
lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 6.
In this unit you buy what you need, and you find your way to it.
Two questions. How much? And which way?
First, how much and how many.
Some things you can count.
One packet. Two packets. Three packets.
Some things you cannot count.
Flour. Oil. Butter.
You cannot say two flours.
For a small number of things you can count, say a few.
A few packets. A few jars. A few people.
For a small amount of a thing you cannot count, say a little.
A little flour. A little oil. A little time.
Listen.
I need a few eggs and a little milk.
There are a few people at the till.
Add a little oil when you cook.
Now drop the a.
Few, with no a, means not many.
Few shops are open early.
Little, with no a, means not much.
There is little time before the shop closes.
A few is friendly. Few is a worry.
And the question word changes too.
How many packets? A few.
How much flour? A little.
Now, each and every.
Each and every both mean all of them.
But they look at them differently.
Each looks at one, then the next one.
Each box has a label.
Every looks at the whole group. Not one is left out.
Every box has a label.
Both lines are true.
Listen.
Look at each of the six jars.
Every jar has the price on the label.
I go to the market every week.
After each and every, the naming word is one, not many.
Not: each boxes. Yes: each box.
Not: every days. Yes: every day.
And the verb takes an s.
Every shop closes at six.
Two small rules to keep.
Before of the, use each. Each of the six packets.
For a time that comes again and again, use every. Every week.
Now, which way.
You already say where a thing is.
Now say which way it goes.
Into: from outside to inside.
I went into the shop.
Out of: from inside to outside.
She came out of the aisle.
Towards: you get nearer to it.
Walk towards the till.
Across: from one side to the other side.
Go across the road.
Along: follow a long thing, like a street or an aisle.
Walk along the aisle.
Through: in one side and out the other.
We walked through the market.
Past: go by it and keep going.
Go past the bank.
Around: all the way round a thing.
Walk around the display.
Listen to the difference.
Into the shop: you are inside now.
Past the shop: you did not stop.
Now the words.
Thirty words, in four groups.
In the shop: display, trolley, basket, aisle, till, label, packet, jar.
How much there is: amount, quantity, several, plenty, portion, piece, dozen, pair.
Things you cannot count: pasta, flour, oil, pepper, butter, cheese.
Which way: into, towards, across, along, through, past, around, direction.
One last thing.
The label tells you the amount. Read it before you pay.
Now go to the words.
Listen, say each one, and check.

outcomes.outcome: Say how much and how many you need, choosing a few or a little for the kind of word, and say this unit's shop words clearly.

outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say how much or how many of a thing I need.

outcomes.outcome: Use each and every with a single naming word and the right verb ending, in speech and in writing.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice self-checked; Practice 2 six or more of eight; Speaking 2 recording; Writing 2 against the model; Quiz items 3 and 4.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write each and every with one naming word after them.

outcomes.outcome: Say which way a person or a thing goes, using into, out of, towards, across, along, through, past and around.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice self-checked; Practice 3 eight or more of ten; Speaking 3 and Speaking 5 recordings; Quiz items 6, 7, 8 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say which way a thing goes, not only where it is.

outcomes.outcome: Read a shop notice and a set of directions, follow them step by step, and work out a shop word from the text around it.
outcomes.evidence: Comprehension items 5 to 10; Practice 5 five or more of six; Practice 6 six or more of eight; Quiz items 5, 9, 10 and 11.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a shop notice and find what I need in it.

words.meaning: A group of things put out at the front, so that people can see them.
words.example: There was a display of jars at the end of the aisle.
practice: Walk around the display and look at the back of it.
The display near the door has the new packets on it.
She took one jar from the display and read the label.
Display has two parts: dis-play.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to describe a display of fruit in three lines. Then describe a display you have seen yourself.

words.meaning: A big basket on wheels. You push it in front of you in a shop.
words.example: I took a trolley, because my list was long.
practice: The trolleys are outside, to the left of the door.
Put the heavy bags in the trolley, not in the basket.
Please push the trolley back after you use it.
Trolley ends in -ey, like money.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor when a trolley is better than a basket. Then give it two reasons of your own.

words.meaning: A light open box that you carry your shopping in.
words.example: Six things fit in a basket.
practice: The baskets are by the door as you go in.
She put the packet of pasta into her basket.
A basket is easier than a trolley for a few things.
Basket has two parts: bas-ket.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor four things in your basket. Ask it to say back how many of each one you named.

words.meaning: A long space between the shelves in a shop. You walk along it.
words.example: The oil is in aisle 2.
practice: Walk along this aisle to the end, then turn left.
Every aisle has a number on a notice at the end.
Which aisle has the flour in it?
In aisle the s is quiet. Say: eye-l.
words.tutor: Say aisle to the tutor three times. Ask it whether it heard an s sound. There should be none.

words.meaning: The place in a shop where you pay.
words.example: There were a few people at the till.
practice: The tills are at the front, past aisle 1.
Put each thing on the counter beside the till.
Walk towards the till when you are ready to pay.
Till has one part, and two l letters at the end.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for four short lines you could say at a till. Say each one back and keep the two you like.

words.meaning: A small piece of paper on a thing. It gives the name, the price and the amount.
words.example: Read the label before you pay.
practice: Every jar has a label on the front.
The label says how many grams are inside.
She looked at each label and compared the prices.
Label has two parts: la-bel.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what three things a food label usually gives. Then say which one you look at first.

words.meaning: A small paper bag with food inside, closed and ready to buy.
words.example: I took two packets of pasta.
practice: A large packet of rice costs less than two small ones.
Open the packet carefully and pour it into the bowl.
How many portions are in one packet?
Packet has two parts: pack-et.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for five foods that come in a packet. Say which of them you buy most weeks.

words.meaning: A small glass thing that holds food. You open the top and close it again.
words.example: She opened the jar and looked inside.
practice: There was a display of jars at the end of aisle 2.
He put the jar into the basket, beside the butter.
A large jar holds more than two small ones.
Jar has one part. It sounds like car with a j.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three foods that come in a jar and three that come in a packet. Then add one of each.

words.meaning: How much of a thing there is. Use it for things you cannot count.
words.example: The label shows the amount inside.
practice: I used a small amount of oil.
What amount of flour does this bread need?
The amount on the label is written in grams.
Amount has two parts: a-mount.
words.starter: I used a small amount of
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for four lines with amount. Say which of them could be about the food in your kitchen.

words.meaning: How much there is, or how many there are. You see it on labels and forms more than you hear it in talk.
words.example: Write the quantity of each thing on your list.
practice: The form asks for the name and the quantity.
A large quantity of rice is cheaper by the kilo.
Quantity works for both kinds of word, and amount does not.
Quantity has three parts: quan-ti-ty.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor the difference between amount and quantity. Then give it one line for each.

words.meaning: More than a few, but not many. About three to six.
words.example: Several people were waiting at the till.
practice: I bought several packets of pasta.
Several jars were open on the display.
She read several labels before she chose one.
Several works with things you can count, never with flour or oil.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to put a few, several and plenty in order, from small to big. Then say a line for each.

words.meaning: More than enough.
words.example: There is plenty of time before the shop closes.
practice: We have plenty of flour at home.
There were plenty of eggs on the shelf.
Plenty of works with both kinds of word: plenty of rice, plenty of jars.
Plenty has two parts: plen-ty.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you have plenty of at home. Ask it to check that you said plenty of each time.

words.meaning: The part of the food for one person.
words.example: This packet holds four portions.
practice: One portion of pasta is about eighty grams.
She put a small portion on each plate.
How many portions does a large jar give?
Portion has two parts: por-tion.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor how a label shows the number of portions. Then say how many portions you cook at a time.

words.meaning: One part of something bigger.
words.example: I cut a piece of cheese for the bread.
practice: Take a piece of paper and write your list on it.
A piece of bread and a little butter is enough.
Cheese comes in one big piece or in small packets.
Piece and peace sound the same, but they mean different things.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for four foods that come in pieces. Then say which of them you cut yourself.

words.meaning: Twelve.
words.example: I bought a dozen eggs.
practice: A dozen is twelve, and half a dozen is six.
The notice says a dozen eggs, and the price is 3.
She counted two dozen jars on the display.
Dozen has two parts: doz-en.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor how many a dozen is and how many half a dozen is. Then say both numbers back.

words.meaning: Two things that go together.
words.example: I need a new pair of scissors.
practice: A pair means two, so a pair of eggs is two eggs.
The shop sells them in pairs, never one by one.
She keeps a pair of scissors in the kitchen.
Pair and pear sound the same, but a pear is a fruit.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for five things that come in a pair. Say which of them you have at home.

words.meaning: A dry food made from flour and water. You boil it in water.
words.example: The pasta is in aisle 1.
practice: Boil the pasta for about ten minutes.
How much pasta do you need for four portions?
There is plenty of pasta in this packet.
Pasta is a word you cannot count. Never say two pastas.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor why we say a little pasta and not a few pastas. Then give it two more words like it.

words.meaning: The soft white food you mix with water to make bread.
words.example: I need a little flour for the bread.
practice: A bag of flour is one kilo.
The flour is in aisle 2, next to the oil.
Pour the flour into a large bowl.
Flour and flower sound the same, but a flower grows in a garden.
words.tutor: Say flour and flower to the tutor. Ask it which one it heard, and try again if it names the wrong one.

words.meaning: A yellow food that pours like water. You use it when you cook.
words.example: Add a little oil when you cook.
practice: The oil is on the shelf below the flour.
A small bottle of oil is enough for a week.
You cannot count oil. Say a little oil, not a few oils.
Oil has one part. It sounds like boil with no b.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three lines with a little oil. Then say one line of your own about cooking.

words.meaning: A dark food with a strong taste. You put a little of it on your food.
words.example: Put a little pepper on the eggs.
practice: There is plenty of pepper in this jar.
The pepper and the salt are on the same shelf.
I do not like a large amount of pepper.
Pepper has two parts: pep-per.
words.starter: I put a little pepper on
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two foods you add pepper to and two you do not. Then say whether you agree.

words.meaning: A soft yellow food made from milk. You put it on bread.
words.example: There is a little butter left in the fridge.
practice: Butter is in aisle 4, next to the cheese.
Put a little butter on the bread, not a lot.
A small piece of butter is enough for the pasta.
Butter has two parts: but-ter.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor why we say a little butter and not a few butters. Then say the rule back in your own words.

words.meaning: A food made from milk. It can be hard or soft.
words.example: The cheese is at the back of the shop.
practice: A little cheese on the pasta is very good.
How much cheese do you need for four people?
Cheese comes in one large piece or in small packets.
Cheese has one part. It ends with a z sound.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for four lines with cheese, two with a little and two with a piece of. Say which two you would use.

words.meaning: From outside to inside.
words.example: I went into the shop and took a basket.
practice: He put the jar into the trolley.
Pour the pasta into the water.
She walked into the aisle and read the labels.
To takes you as far as the door. Into takes you inside.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two lines with to and two with into. Say what changes between them.

words.meaning: Moving so that you get nearer to something.
words.example: Walk towards the till when you are ready to pay.
practice: I could not read the notice, so I walked towards it.
The trolleys are over there. Go towards the door.
Towards does not always mean all the way. You can stop before you arrive.
Towards has two parts: to-wards.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor the difference between to the door and towards the door. Then use each one in a line.

words.meaning: From one side to the other side.
words.example: The shop is across the road from the bus stop.
practice: Go across the bridge and turn left.
Walk across the shop to reach aisle 4.
Use the crossing when you go across the road.
Across has two parts: a-cross.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three lines with across. Then say one about the street where you live.

words.meaning: Following a long thing, such as a street or an aisle.
words.example: Walk along the aisle to the end.
practice: The new stop is fifty metres along the road.
Go along this street, past the bank.
Along follows a long line. Across cuts over it.
Along has two parts: a-long.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you directions that use along twice. Then say the same directions in your own words.

words.meaning: In one side and out the other side.
words.example: Go through the door and turn left.
practice: The way out is through the second door.
We walked through the market to the bus stop.
Through means in one side and out the other. Past means you do not go in.
In through the g and the h are quiet. Say: throo.
words.tutor: Say through to the tutor five times. Ask it whether the word had two sounds at the end. It should not.

words.meaning: Going by something and not stopping.
words.example: Go past the bank and keep walking.
practice: The tills are at the front, past aisle 1.
I walked past the café and went into the shop.
Past means you do not stop. Into means you go inside.
Past and passed sound the same.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for one line with past and one with into about the same shop. Say which one means you bought something.

words.meaning: All the way round something.
words.example: There is a display in the middle. Walk around it.
practice: She pushed the trolley around the shop.
Go around the corner and you will see the till.
Around goes round the outside. Through goes in one side and out the other.
Around has two parts: a-round.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two lines with around and two with through. Then say which word fits a display in the middle.

words.meaning: The way something moves, or the way you must go.
words.example: Which direction is the market from here?
practice: The notice gives directions to every aisle.
We were walking in the wrong direction.
Ask the person at the till for directions.
Direction has three parts: di-rec-tion.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for directions from a bus stop to a shop. Then say them back and count the steps.

grammar.title: A few packets, a little flour
grammar.explanation:
Some things you can count: packets, jars, eggs.
Some things you cannot count: flour, oil, butter.
For a small number of things you can count, say a few.
For a small amount of a thing you cannot count, say a little.
Drop the a and the meaning turns: few means not many, little means not much.
grammar.rule:
Count them: a few.
a few packets
a few jars
a few people

Cannot count them: a little.
a little flour
a little oil
a little time

The question word changes too.
How many packets? A few.
How much flour? A little.

With no a, it is a worry:
Few shops are open early. (not many)
There is little time left. (not much)

Two more words from this unit:
several: more than a few, and only for things you count.
plenty of: more than enough, and for both kinds.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: you need a small amount of oil and a small number of eggs.
1. Eggs. Can you count them? Yes. One egg, two eggs.
2. So use a few: a few eggs.
3. Oil. Can you count it? No. Two oils is not English.
4. So use a little: a little oil.
5. Put them together: I need a few eggs and a little oil.
6. Check the s. Eggs has one. Oil has none. Correct.
7. Check the question: How many eggs? How much oil?
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use a little for things you can count.
No: I need a little eggs.
Yes: I need a few eggs.
The test is short. If you can say two of them, use a few.
grammar.tip: Count them: a few. Pour them: a little.
grammar.practice:
Write a few or a little.
1. I need ___ flour for the bread.
2. There are ___ people at the till.
3. Add ___ oil when you cook.
4. She bought ___ jars of pepper.
5. We have ___ time before the shop closes.
6. There are ___ packets left on the display.
7. Put ___ butter on the bread.
grammar.answers:
1. a little  2. a few  3. a little  4. a few  5. a little  6. a few  7. a little
Wrong on 1, 3 or 7? Flour, oil and butter have no plural s. You cannot count them, so they take a little.
Wrong on 5? Time is not counted here either.
Wrong on 2, 4 or 6? People, jars and packets all have a plural s, so they take a few.
Six or seven right: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

grammar.title: Each box, every day
grammar.explanation:
Each and every both mean all of them.
Each looks at one, then the next one.
Every looks at the whole group. Not one is left out.
After both of them the naming word is one, not many.
And the verb takes an s: every shop closes at six.
grammar.rule:
Each: one, then the next.
Look at each jar.
Each box has a label.

Every: the whole group.
Every jar has a price on it.
Every shop closes at six.

After each and every: one thing.
each box, not each boxes
every day, not every days

The verb takes an s:
Each aisle has a number.
Every label shows the amount.

Two rules you can hold on to:
Before of the, use each: each of the six packets.
For a time that comes again and again, use every: every week, every morning, every time.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: say that all six packets have a label, in two ways.
1. Start with the group: six packets.
2. One at a time: each packet.
3. Is packet one thing or many? One. So: each packet.
4. The verb takes an s: each packet has a label.
5. Now the whole group: every packet has a label.
6. Check: no plural s on packet in either line. Correct.
7. Now put of the in: the price on each of the six packets.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put a plural s after each and every.
No: every days. No: each boxes.
Yes: every day. Yes: each box.
Each and every take one thing, even when you mean all of them.
grammar.tip: Each: one, then the next. Every: all of them, none left out.
grammar.practice:
Write each or every.
1. I go to the market ___ week.
2. She lifted the jars out of the basket, ___ one in turn.
3. The price on ___ of the six packets is the same.
4. Open the shop ___ morning at eight.
5. Look at ___ of the three labels and compare them.
6. I check the label ___ time I buy flour.
7. Write this line again with no plural s: Every boxes has a label.
8. Choose the right verb: Every shop (close / closes) at six.
grammar.answers:
1. every  2. each  3. each  4. every  5. each  6. every
7. Every box has a label.
8. closes
Items 1, 4 and 6 are times that come again and again, so they take every. Every time is a pair you will hear often.
Items 3 and 5 come before of the, and only each works there.
Item 2 says one in turn, which is what each means.
Wrong on 7? Every takes one thing, so boxes loses its s.
Wrong on 8? Every shop is one shop at a time, so the verb takes an s.
Six or more of eight: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

grammar.title: Into the shop, across the road, past the bank
grammar.explanation:
These words say which way a thing goes.
They do not say where it is. They say the way it moves.
Each one draws a different line.
Into goes inside. Past goes by and keeps going.
Draw the line with your finger, then pick the word.
grammar.rule:
into: outside to inside
I went into the shop.

out of: inside to outside
She came out of the aisle.

towards: you get nearer to it
Walk towards the till.

across: one side to the other side
Go across the road.

along: follow a long thing
Walk along the aisle.

through: in one side and out the other
We walked through the market.

past: go by it and keep going
Go past the bank.

around: all the way round
Walk around the display.

from: the place you start
I walked from the station.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: you start at the station. The shop is on the other side of the road, after the bank.
1. Where do you start? The station. That takes from: from the station.
2. The road is long and you follow it. That is along: walk along the road.
3. The bank is on the way and you do not stop. That is past: past the bank.
4. The shop is on the other side, so you cross. That is across: across the road.
5. Now you go inside. That is into: into the shop.
6. In order: From the station, walk along the road, past the bank.
7. Then: Go across the road and into the shop.
8. Check: does every word draw a different line? Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to say to when you mean into.
No: I went to the shop and looked at the display inside.
Yes: I went into the shop and looked at the display.
To takes you as far as the door. Into takes you inside.
grammar.tip: Draw the line with your finger first. Then pick the word.
grammar.practice:
Write into, out of, towards, across, along, through, past or around. Use every word at least once. Two of them are used twice.
1. The bus goes ___ the bridge and stops on the other side.
2. Walk ___ the aisle until you reach the end.
3. She took the packet ___ her basket and put it on the counter.
4. Go ___ the door and turn left.
5. He put the jar ___ the trolley.
6. The bank is on this street. Walk ___ it and keep going.
7. There is a display in the middle. Walk ___ it.
8. I could not read the notice, so I walked ___ it.
9. We came ___ the shop with two heavy bags.
10. Push the trolley ___ the shop to aisle 4.
grammar.answers:
1. across  2. along  3. out of  4. through  5. into  6. past  7. around  8. towards  9. out of  10. across
Item 1 crosses from one side to the other, so it is across. Item 10 crosses the shop in the same way.
Items 3 and 9 both go from inside to outside, so they take out of.
Wrong on 4? Through goes in one side of the door and out the other. Past would take you by the door without going in.
Wrong on 7? Around goes all the way round the outside of the display.
Wrong on 8? Towards means you got nearer to the notice. It does not say you reached it.
Eight or more of ten: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

readings.title: Six Things on the List
readings.setting: A short shop before work, on an ordinary weekday morning.
readings.passage:
I had six things on my list, and twenty minutes before work.
The shop is across the road from the bus stop.
I went into the shop and took a basket, not a trolley.
Six things fit in a basket.
The first aisle had the pasta and the flour.
I took two packets of pasta and a bag of flour.
I needed a little oil, so I took the small bottle.
Then I walked along the aisle towards the cheese.
There was a display of jars at the end. I walked around it.
Every jar had the price on the label.
I read each label before I put it in the basket.
The price on the large jar of pepper was 5. On the small one it was 3.
I took the small one, because I use very little pepper.
Then I went past the bread and straight to the till.
There were a few people in front of me.
I paid, and I still had eight minutes.

readings.title: How a Big Shop Is Laid Out
readings.setting: A short help page about finding your way round a large food shop.
readings.passage:
A big shop is laid out in long lines. Each line is called an aisle.
Every aisle has a number and a notice at the end.
The notice says what is in that aisle: pasta, oil, tea.
Walk along an aisle to look at everything in it.
Walk across the shop to move from one aisle to another.
Bread and fruit are often near the door.
Milk, butter and cheese are often at the back.
This is not an accident. You walk past many other things on the way.
Take a basket for a few things. Take a trolley for a big shop.
Every packet and every jar has a label on it.
The label shows the amount inside, in grams.
It also shows the price for one kilo, in small print.
That number is useful, because it lets you compare two sizes.
A large packet is not always the better price.
At the till, put each thing on the counter.
The person at the till will tell you the price.

readings.title: Notice Inside the Door
readings.setting: A printed notice on the wall just inside the door of a food shop.
readings.passage:
WELCOME. PLEASE READ.

WHERE THINGS ARE
Aisle 1: bread, pasta, rice
Aisle 2: oil, flour, sugar, pepper
Aisle 3: tea, coffee, biscuits
Aisle 4: milk, butter, cheese, eggs
Tills: at the front, past aisle 1.

BASKETS AND TROLLEYS
The baskets are by this door.
The trolleys are outside, to the left.
Please push the trolley back after you use it.

THIS WEEK
A dozen eggs: the price is 3.
Two packets of pasta: the price is 5.
Every label shows the price for one kilo.

IF YOU CANNOT FIND SOMETHING
Walk towards the till at the front.
Ask the person there. They will tell you the aisle.

THE WAY OUT
Go past the tills and through the second door.

comprehension.q: Why did the writer take a basket and not a trolley?
comprehension.a: Because there were only six things on the list, and six things fit in a basket.
comprehension.why: Line 3 says basket, not trolley, and line 4 gives the reason: six things fit in a basket.

comprehension.q: The writer walked around the display. What does around mean here?
comprehension.a: All the way round the outside of it.
comprehension.why: The display was at the end of the aisle, in the way. The writer went round the outside of it, not through it.

comprehension.q: The writer took the small jar of pepper. Give the two reasons in the text.
comprehension.a: The small jar cost less, and the writer uses very little pepper.
comprehension.why: The two prices are given in one line, 5 and 3, and the next line says the writer uses very little pepper.

comprehension.q: How many people were in front of the writer at the till?
comprehension.why: The text says a few people, which is a small number of things you can count.

comprehension.q: What does the notice at the end of an aisle tell you?
comprehension.a: What is in that aisle, such as pasta, oil or tea.
comprehension.why: The third line names the notice and gives three examples of what it lists.

comprehension.q: From this text, what is an aisle?
comprehension.a: One of the long lines in a shop, that you walk along.
comprehension.why: The first line says a big shop is laid out in long lines. It then says each line is called an aisle.

comprehension.q: You want to know whether the large packet is the better price. What does the text tell you to look at?
comprehension.a: The price for one kilo, in small print on the label.
comprehension.why: The text says that number lets you compare two sizes. It adds that a large packet is not always the better price.

comprehension.q: You need flour and butter. Which aisle do you go to for each one?
comprehension.a: Aisle 2 for the flour, and aisle 4 for the butter.
comprehension.why: Flour is listed under aisle 2 and butter under aisle 4, in the part headed WHERE THINGS ARE.

comprehension.q: You have a long list and you want a trolley. Where do you go?
comprehension.a: Outside, to the left of the door.
comprehension.why: The notice says the baskets are by that door and the trolleys are outside, to the left.

comprehension.q: You have paid. Which way do you leave the shop?
comprehension.a: Go past the tills and through the second door.
comprehension.why: That is the only line under the heading THE WAY OUT, and it gives both steps in order.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — A few, or a little?
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I need a few eggs and a little milk.
There are a few people at the till.
Add a little oil when you cook.
She bought a few jars of pepper.
There is a little butter left in the fridge.
Now say four lines of your own about food you buy.
Use a few twice and a little twice.
Tap the mic. Say your four lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: does every a few word end in s?
Check: does every a little word have no s?
speaking.tutor: Say four lines to the tutor, two with a few and two with a little. Ask it to name the words that had a plural s.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Each and every out loud
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
Each box has a label.
Every jar has the price on it.
I go to the market every week.
Look at each of the six packets.
Every shop on this street closes at six.
Now say four lines of your own.
Use each twice and every twice.
Tap the mic. Say your four lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: is the naming word after each and every one thing, with no s?
Check: does the verb end in s?
speaking.tutor: Say four lines to the tutor, two with each and two with every. Ask it whether any naming word had a plural s.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Which way does it go?
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I went into the shop.
She came out of the aisle.
Walk towards the till.
Go across the road.
Walk along the aisle.
We walked through the market.
Go past the bank.
Walk around the display.
Now draw each line in the air with your finger as you say it.
Tap the mic. Say all eight lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: can you hear eight different words?
Check: did into and past sound different from each other?
speaking.tutor: Say the eight lines to the tutor. Ask it to name the eight direction words it heard, in order.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — The shop words, part by part
speaking.instructions:
Some of this unit's words hide a quiet letter. Listen and repeat.
aisle: the s is quiet. Say: eye-l.
through: the g and the h are quiet. Say: throo.
Now the long words. Say them in parts.
quan-ti-ty
por-tion
se-ve-ral
di-rec-tion
trol-ley
Now two pairs that sound the same.
flour and flower
piece and peace
Tap the mic. Say the two quiet-letter words, the five long words and the two pairs.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: is there any s sound in aisle? There should be none.
Check: can you hear three parts in quantity and in direction?
speaking.tutor: Say aisle, through, quantity and direction to the tutor. Ask it which word it heard each time, and say again the ones it got wrong.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Give the way in five steps
speaking.instructions:
Here are directions from a bus stop to a shop. Listen.
Come out of the bus stop and go across the road.
Walk along the road towards the bank.
Go past the bank and around the corner.
The shop is on your left. Go in through the first door.
The flour is in aisle 2, halfway along on the right.
Now give directions of your own, in five steps.
A made-up street and a made-up shop are fine.
Use a different direction word in each step.
Tap the mic. Say your five steps.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: five steps, five different direction words?
Check: could somebody follow them without asking you anything?
speaking.tutor: Say your five steps to the tutor. Ask it to say back only the direction words, in order, and check them against yours.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Ask in the shop, then answer
speaking.instructions:
Five questions. Listen, then say each one.
Where is the flour, please?
Which aisle is the cheese in?
How much pasta do I need for four people?
How many eggs are in a packet?
Is there another way out?
Now the answers. Listen, then say each one.
It is in aisle 2, along on the left.
The cheese is in aisle 4, at the back.
You need about four portions, so one packet.
There are a dozen, so twelve.
Yes. Go past the tills and through the second door.
Tap the mic. Ask the five questions, then answer them yourself.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: does every answer match its question?
Check: did you use how much for flour and pasta, and how many for eggs?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to put the five questions to you, one at a time. Answer each one, then ask it the same five back.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A shopping list with amounts
writing.prompt:
Write a shopping list of eight things by hand, on paper.
A made-up list is fine.
Give the amount for every thing: a number, a packet, a jar, a piece, a dozen or a little.
Lay it out like the model: a heading, then one thing on each line.
writing.model:
SHOPPING, SATURDAY
2 packets of pasta
a little flour, about half a kilo
1 small bottle of oil
1 jar of pepper
a dozen eggs
a piece of cheese, about 300 grams
a little butter
4 apples
writing.criteria:
A heading in capital letters at the top.
Eight lines, with one thing on each line.
An amount on every line.
At least two lines use a little.
Written by hand, and every word still readable when you look at it again tomorrow.
writing.support:
Write the eight things first, with no amounts.
Then go back down the list and ask one question at each line: can I count this?
If yes, write a number, a packet or a dozen. If no, write a little.
writing.extension: Write the list again on one side of a small piece of paper, so it fits in your hand.

writing.title: Writing 2 — What I check every time
writing.prompt:
Write six lines about what you check when you shop.
Use each in three lines and every in three lines.
A made-up shop is fine.
writing.model:
I read every label before I pay.
I look at each of the two sizes and compare the prices.
Every jar has the price for one kilo on it, in small print.
I check each date, because the milk at the front is often the oldest.
I count every packet in the basket before I go to the till.
I put each heavy thing at the bottom of the bag.
writing.criteria:
Six sentences.
Three with each and three with every.
One naming word after each and every, with no plural s.
Every verb after each and every ends in s where it should.
One line uses each of the.
writing.support:
Take one line only.
Write the thing you check: the label.
Now put every in front of it: every label.
Now add what you do: I read every label before I pay.
Do the other five the same way.
writing.extension: Add a seventh line that begins: Every time I buy flour, I

writing.title: Writing 3 — Directions in numbered steps
writing.prompt:
Write directions from a bus stop to a shop, in five numbered steps, by hand.
A made-up street is fine.
Use a different direction word in every step.
Lay it out like the model: a heading, then one numbered step on each line.
writing.model:
FROM THE BUS STOP TO THE SHOP
1. Come out of the bus stop and turn left.
2. Walk along the road for about two minutes.
3. Go past the bank and the café.
4. Go across the road at the crossing.
5. The shop is on your right. Go in through the first door.
writing.length: A heading and five numbered steps
writing.criteria:
A heading at the top.
Five steps, numbered 1 to 5, one on each line.
A different direction word in each step.
Every step starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
Written by hand, and still readable when you read it back tomorrow.
writing.support:
Draw the way first, as a line on paper, with the bus stop at one end.
Mark the places you go by: the bank, the corner, the road.
Then write one step for each mark, and add the direction word last.
writing.extension: Add a sixth step that says which aisle the flour is in.

writing.title: Writing 4 — The shop trip
writing.prompt:
Write six lines about a shop trip.
A made-up trip is fine.
Say which way you went, what you bought and how much of each thing.
Join the lines with then, after that and because.
writing.model:
On Saturday I went across the road to the shop.
I took a basket, because I only had six things on my list.
I walked along the first aisle and took two packets of pasta.
Then I needed a little flour and a little oil, so I went to aisle 2.
After that I walked past the display of jars and around the corner to the cheese.
I paid at the till, and there were only a few people in front of me.
writing.criteria:
Six sentences, in the order it happened.
At least three different direction words.
At least one line with a few and one with a little.
At least two joining words from then, after that and because.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
writing.support:
List six steps in single words first, in order.
Like this: crossed, basket, pasta, flour, cheese, paid.
Then write one line for each word, and add the joining words last.
writing.extension: Add a seventh line that says how long the trip took, and one thing you forgot.

activities.title: Practice 1 — A few or a little?
activities.instructions:
Write a few or a little.
1. There is only ___ oil left in the bottle.
2. I bought ___ packets of pasta.
3. Put ___ pepper on the eggs.
4. ___ people were waiting at the till.
5. We need ___ flour for the bread.
6. She took ___ jars from the display.
7. There is ___ butter in the fridge.
8. I have ___ minutes before the bus comes.
9. Add ___ cheese to the pasta.
10. There were ___ labels with no price on them.
activities.answers:
1. a little  2. a few  3. a little  4. A few  5. a little  6. a few  7. a little  8. a few  9. a little  10. a few
The test is short: if the word has a plural s, use a few.
Wrong on 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9? Oil, pepper, flour, butter and cheese have no plural s, so they take a little.
Wrong on 8? Minutes has an s, so it takes a few.
Eight or more of ten: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 1 again and mark it once more.
activities.solo: Write your answers on paper first. Then mark them with the key and count them. Read the ten lines out loud.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Each or every?
activities.instructions:
Write each or every.
1. I go to this shop ___ Saturday.
2. Look at ___ of the four labels and compare the prices.
3. ___ aisle has a notice at the end.
4. She read ___ label in turn, one after the other.
5. The price on ___ of the six jars is the same.
6. I check the date ___ time I buy milk.
7. Open the shop ___ morning at eight.
8. ___ packet in the basket has the amount on it.
activities.answers:
1. every  2. each  3. Every  4. each  5. each  6. every  7. every  8. Every
Items 1, 6 and 7 are times that come again and again, so they take every.
Items 2 and 5 come before of the, where only each works.
Item 4 says in turn, one after the other, which is what each means.
Items 3 and 8 are about the whole group, with none left out, so every fits.
Six or more of eight: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 2 again.
activities.solo: Cover the answers. Write each or every for all eight. Then mark them and read the full lines out loud.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Which way?
activities.instructions:
Write into, out of, towards, across, along, through, past or around.
1. Push the trolley ___ the aisle to the end.
2. She took the jar ___ the basket and put it on the counter.
3. The bank is on this street. Walk ___ it and keep going.
4. Go ___ the door and turn right.
5. He put two packets ___ his basket.
6. The shop is on the other side. Go ___ the road at the crossing.
7. There is a display in the middle. Walk ___ it.
8. I could not read the notice, so I walked ___ it.
9. The way out is ___ the second door.
10. Walk ___ the shop, from aisle 1 to aisle 4.
activities.answers:
1. along  2. out of  3. past  4. through  5. into  6. across  7. around  8. towards  9. through  10. across
Wrong on 1 or 10? Along follows a long line. Across cuts over it.
Wrong on 3? Past means you go by the bank and do not stop.
Wrong on 4 or 9? Through goes in one side of the door and out the other.
Wrong on 5? Into goes from outside to inside. To would stop you at the edge.
Wrong on 8? Towards means you got nearer to the notice, and does not say you reached it.
Eight or more of ten: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 3 again and mark it once more.
activities.solo: Write the ten words on paper and mark them with the key. Copy out the whole line for any you got wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Can you count it?
activities.instructions:
Write each word under one of two headings.
Headings: I can count it. I cannot count it.
Words: flour, packet, oil, jar, pasta, basket, butter, aisle, cheese, label, pepper, trolley, portion, milk, display, egg.
activities.answers:
I can count it: packet, jar, basket, aisle, label, trolley, portion, display, egg
I cannot count it: flour, oil, pasta, butter, cheese, pepper, milk
The test is the plural s. Two packets is English. Two flours is not.
The first group takes a few, several and how many.
The second group takes a little, plenty of and how much.
Careful with cheese and pasta: you can buy two packets of them, but you still cannot count the food itself.
Fourteen or more of sixteen: go on. Fewer? Go back to the word list and listen to each one again.
activities.solo: Write the two headings on paper and put each word under one. Then check with the key and say a few or a little in front of every word.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the notice
activities.instructions:
Read the Notice Inside the Door again. Then answer in a few words.
1. Which aisle has the pepper in it?
2. You want tea and biscuits. Which aisle?
3. Where do you find a basket?
4. What is the price of a dozen eggs this week?
5. You cannot find the rice. What does the notice tell you to do?
6. Where are the tills?
activities.answers:
1. Aisle 2  2. Aisle 3  3. By the door, inside  4. The price is 3  5. Walk towards the till at the front and ask the person there  6. At the front, past aisle 1
Wrong on 1? Pepper is on the aisle 2 line, after oil, flour and sugar.
Wrong on 3? The baskets are by that door, and only the trolleys are outside.
Wrong on 5? The notice gives one instruction under IF YOU CANNOT FIND SOMETHING, and it has two steps: walk towards the till, then ask.
Five or six right: go on. Fewer? Read the notice one heading at a time and answer again.
activities.solo: Cover the notice and answer from memory first. Then open it, mark your answers and put a line under the part that gave you each one.

activities.title: Practice 6 — How much there is
activities.instructions:
Choose amount, quantity, several, plenty, portion, piece, dozen or pair. Use each word once.
1. Twelve eggs is a ___.
2. Two things that go together are a ___.
3. More than enough is ___ of.
4. More than a few, but not many, is ___.
5. The food for one person is one ___.
6. One part of something bigger is a ___.
7. How much of a thing there is, for things you cannot count, is the ___.
8. The word on a label or a form for how much or how many is the ___.
activities.answers:
1. dozen  2. pair  3. plenty  4. several  5. portion  6. piece  7. amount  8. quantity
Wrong on 7 or 8? Amount is for things you cannot count. Quantity works for both kinds, and you see it written more than you hear it.
Wrong on 4? Several is only for things you can count, so it never goes with flour or oil.
Wrong on 5 or 6? A portion is the food for one person. A piece is one part cut off something bigger.
Six or more of eight: go on. Fewer? Read the How much there is group again.
activities.solo: Write the eight words on paper, one for each line. Then mark them with the key and read each full sentence out loud.

quizzes.why: Flour has no plural s, so it takes a little. Eggs has one, so it takes a few. The second option turns the pair round, and the last two use one word for both kinds.

options: I need a little of egg.
quizzes.why: Eggs can be counted, so a few fits. The first uses a little for a counted word. The third uses a few for flour, which you cannot count. The fourth adds an of that does not belong.
After every, the naming word is one thing, and the verb takes an s. The first two put a plural s on the naming word. The last one drops the s from the verb.

quizzes.q: The price on ___ of the six packets is the same.
quizzes.why: Before of the, English uses each. Every cannot stand before of the. All would need a plural verb: all of the six packets are the same. Much is for things you cannot count.

quizzes.q: The notice says: a dozen eggs. How many eggs is that?
quizzes.why: A dozen is twelve. Six is half a dozen. Ten and twenty are round numbers, but neither is what dozen means.

quizzes.q: You want to get from one side of the road to the other. Which word?
quizzes.why: Across goes from one side to the other side. Along follows the road instead of cutting over it, past takes you by something, and into takes you inside.

quizzes.q: The bank is on your street. You do not stop there. Which word?
quizzes.why: Past means you go by it and keep going. Into and through would both take you inside the bank, and around would send you all the way round it.

quizzes.q: He put the jar ___ the trolley.
quizzes.why: The jar goes from outside the trolley to inside it, so into fits. The other three all move by, over or beside a thing, and none of them ends up inside.

options: A long space between the shelves, that you walk along.
The place in a shop where you pay.
A small glass thing that holds food.
A paper bag with food inside.
quizzes.a: A long space between the shelves, that you walk along.
quizzes.why: The other three are shop words from this unit too. The till is where you pay. A jar is glass, and a packet is a paper bag.

quizzes.q: The notice says the tills are at the front, past aisle 1. Where are the tills?
options: Outside the shop, to the left.
At the back, beside the milk.
quizzes.why: Past aisle 1 means you go by aisle 1 and keep going, so the tills come after it. Outside to the left is where the trolleys are, and the milk is in aisle 4 at the back.

quizzes.q: Which word means more than enough?
quizzes.why: Plenty of means more than enough. Several is about three to six, a portion is the food for one person, and a dozen is exactly twelve.

quizzes.q: There is a display in the middle of the shop, and you walk all the way round it. Which word?
quizzes.why: Around goes all the way round the outside. Through would take you in one side and out the other. Into would put you inside it. Along follows a long line, such as an aisle.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. If you are helping, play the recording together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence. The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner here and is never the only check on any task.

The counted and uncounted split is the hinge of the whole unit, and the usual slip is a little with a plural word: a little eggs. The repair is a test the learner can run alone, and it is written into the card and into Practice 4: if the word can take a plural s, it takes a few, several and how many; if it cannot, it takes a little, plenty of and how much. Practice 4 sorts sixteen words into the two groups before any sentence is asked for, so a learner who is still unsure can go back to it rather than guessing through the gap fills.

teacherNotes.type: Each and every overlap, and the unit says so
teacherNotes.note: In real English each and every are often both correct, and a card that pretended otherwise would teach a rule the learner would hear broken the next day. So the practice tests only the places where one of them is forced: before of the, only each works; for a time that comes round again and again, only every works; after both, the naming word stays single and the verb takes an s. The free choice between them is shown in the rule as two true lines, not tested as a right and a wrong answer.

No task asks for a real name, a real address, a real shop or a real amount of money. Every list, street and trip in the writing tasks says a made-up one is fine, and prices appear as bare numbers with no currency anywhere. Keep that wording. Writing 1 and Writing 3 are written by hand on paper, so the only record is the learner's own sheet, and the check on them is whether the learner can still read the writing the next day.

The two source units were about maths, measuring, food and health for children. The measuring words, the four operations, the silent b and g spellings, the -ful and -less endings and the health content are all dropped. What is kept is the language underneath: amounts, quantities and the words for moving from one place to another, moved into a shop an adult uses. Some, any, many, much and a lot of are Level 1 Unit 17, and in, on, at, near, next to, above, below, inside, outside and under are Level 1 Units 3 and 15; all of them are used freely here and get no card. Left, right and straight on are Level 1 Unit 15, so this unit's third card teaches only the words that say which way a thing moves.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say how much or how many of a thing I need.
I can write each and every with one naming word after them.
I can say which way a thing goes, not only where it is.
I can read a shop notice and find what I need in it.
I can write a list and numbered steps by hand, and read them back.
I can write a short account of a shop trip in joined sentences.
I can follow spoken directions and hear how much of each thing is wanted.
I can ask where a thing is and how much of it I need.

assignment.title: The list and the way there
assignment.instructions:
Two parts. A made-up shop, street and list are all fine.
1. Write a shopping list of eight things by hand, like Writing 1. Give the amount on every line, and use a little on at least two of them. Under the list, write five numbered steps from a bus stop to that shop, like Writing 3, with a different direction word in each step.
2. Tap the mic. Read your five steps out loud, then say what you will buy and how much of each thing. Use a few at least twice and a little at least twice.
Read your list and your steps out loud once before you send them, and listen to your recording once.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a handwritten list
